Official Forestry outside-forest circular: 3.3 km, 1–1.5 hours, grade 3. Starts on the Gerakies–Kykkos road near Tree Tops hotel. Climbs to Kavallos fire lookout with views over Paphos forest and Marathasa Valley; loops through Gerakies village. Steep start; exposed ridgelines—best in winter.

A quiet path, chosen among locals. Near Vavatsinia, the trail follows a scenic forest road before narrowing into woodland. At the end: a mysterious cave—Venetian-era mine for gold and copper. Do not enter; it goes deep and is unmaintained. The cave marks the turnaround. Easy, beginner-friendly. Limited parking.

Probably the greenest trail in Cyprus. Kampos and Tsakistras area—moss-covered path, dense vegetation, towering trees. First leg: narrow descent through forest; second leg: gravel road with Troodos views. Linear; can do one-way with a car at each end. Secluded. Winter adds snow on the peaks. Best in February for the moss.

Remote ridge on the Kykkos–Tsakistra road. A refuge at the start—jewelry hidden in plain sight. First section: ridgeline with continuous views; then mountain peaks, gravel road toward Kampos or Tsakistra. Park at both ends for one-way, or out-and-back. Best in winter; cloudy days add atmosphere. Shares area with Gnafkio.

E4 European long-distance trail through Machairas Forest. Kionia picnic site (1,240 m) or Profitis Elias (700 m)—start from either. Pine, golden oak, historic charcoal kilns, abandoned 12th-century monastery. Views of Larnaca and Nicosia. One of Cyprus's most beautiful trails. Winter: crisp air, fewer people.

Hidden and unknown. Next to Kykkos Monastery, this trail dives into unspoiled Paphos forest. V-shaped: steep descent, streams at the bottom, steep ascent to Konizi. Dense forest, panoramic views, streams. Do not hike alone. Winter preferred—snakes in warm months. Very difficult; rocky, slippery in rain. Six hours for 14 km round trip.

Remote Cedar Valley. Linear trail through endemic cedar and pine; Trypilos fire lookout at 1,400 m offers 360° views. Parking for 6–7 cars. Part of E4. Winter can bring snow and fog. The cedars are the draw—horizontal layers, distinctive. Access via Panagia or Kykkos.

Unofficial loop near Moniatis. Waterfall cascading 7 m, cold river, Timiou Prodromou Monastery (15th century). Mostly dirt roads; family-friendly. Pine and walnut forest. Winter: mild; good for a capital escape. About 30 km from Limassol. Combine with Saittas or Krasochoria wineries.

Circular trail around the cliffside Stavrovouni Monastery. Punishing ascents, technical descents, rocky terrain. Steep and demanding. Rewards: 360° views of Larnaca, Salt Lake, Mediterranean, Troodos, Famagusta. Best in winter; fully exposed, no shade. Combine with Agia Varvara for ~10 km. Hiking poles recommended.

Short but brutal. Steep ascent from Agia Varvara Monastery to Stavrovouni peak. 280 m gain in 2.4 km. Rocky, sometimes very steep. Rewards: panoramic views of Larnaca, Salt Lake, coastline. Thirty minutes from Larnaca. Combine with Stavrovouni loop for ~10 km. Good training ground.

Circular trail from Vavatsinia—one of Larnaca's highest villages—through Machairas forest. First leg: nature path, dense forest, panoramic views (Limassol south, Morphou north). Second leg: paved road back. Can combine with Moutti tis Athasias for +4.4 km. Winter fog adds a mystic quality.

White cliffs, endless blue. Pissouri—a coastal hike unlike any forest trail. Steepest white cliffs in Cyprus, ~250 m. The path runs a few metres back from the edge; safe but dramatic. No shade—best in winter. Linear out-and-back. Start near Columbia Beach hotel. Different kind of hike.

Circular route from Foinikaria. Pine forest, Germasogeia reservoir, climb to Kyparissia Peak (~760 m). Views to the coast. Birdlife: coal tits, goldfinches, buzzards. Krasochoria wine route nearby. No water on route—bring plenty. Winter: cool and pleasant.

Official Cape Greco circular: 4.8 km, about 2 hours, grade 1. Start at Konnos beach, Agioi Anargyroi church, or the Visitor Centre. Coastal scrub to the church over a sea cave, then Kamara tou Koraka natural bridge and Aphrodite temple ruins. Juniper, wild olive, carob. Part of the E4. Year-round winter sun classic.

Official Cape Greco linear: 4 km, about 1.5 hours, grade 1. Sea Caves to Agioi Anargyroi church (or reverse). Rocky shoreline, then scrub to Kamara tou Koraka natural bridge. E4 path. Connects to Konnos–Agioi Anargyroi and Aphrodite (Cape Greco) trails. Winter means fewer crowds.

Official Forestry linear: 4.5 km downhill, about 2 hours, grade 1 (1,330–930 m). Starts on the Platres–Prodromos road ~400 m from Trooditissa Monastery; ends outside Phini. Calabrian pine, strawberry tree, golden oak. Chantara waterfall (~8 m) after crossing Trooditissa River. Forest road open to traffic—stay alert. Natura 2000.

Official Forestry linear: about 6–6.2 km, 2.5 hours, grade 2 (1,500–1,300 m). Starts at the Department of Forests playground in Prodromos. First ~3 km uphill, then downhill to Zoumi with two finish options on the Pedoulas–Kakopetria road. Black pine, Marathasa and Morphou Bay views. Connects to Prodromos Dam–Stavroulia. Natura 2000.

Official Forestry linear: about 5.2–5.5 km, 2 hours, grade 3 (1,600–1,300 m). Starts ~200 m after Prodromos Dam on the Prodromos–Troodos Square road. Steep downhill; risk of slipping. Ancient black pines (some 500+ years), flora signs, Natura 2000 Forestry College forest. Shares sections with Prodromos–Zoumi; two finishes toward Pedoulas–Kakopetria.

Official Forestry circular: 9 km, about 4 hours, grade 3 (1,690–1,190 m). Starts on the Moniatis–Troodos road near Psilo Dentro (Pano Platres). Calabrian then black pine; views to Kourris Dam, Limassol, and wine villages. Tiring ups and downs throughout. Natura 2000 Troodos National Forest Park.

Official Forestry linear: 9 km downhill, about 3.5 hours, grade 3 (1,655–870 m). From Karvounas–Troodos road (~1 km before Troodos Square) via closed chromium mine at Kannoures, then along Karkotis River crossings on wet stones. Ends at UNESCO Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis beside the bottling plant. Black pine to Calabrian pine. Natura 2000.

Official Forestry linear: 3 km, about 1 hour, grade 2 (1,000–700 m). Between Pelendri (Trimiklini–Pelendri road) and Fylagra on the Saittas–Kato Amiantos road. Historic vineyard path; ~2 km private land, ~1 km Moni State Forest. Views to Limassol bay and Kourris Dam. Recovering Calabrian pine after the 2007 fire. Local winery ~250 m west near Fylagra.

Official Cape Greco circular: 1.7 km, about 45 minutes, grade 1. From Konnos beach parking along the rugged shore to Spilia tou Kyklopa (Cyclops Cave), then return via beach path. Turquoise Konnos and Agioi Anargyroi views. Part of the E4. Year-round classic.

Official Cape Greco circular: 2 km, about 1 hour, grade 1. Starts at the Visitor Centre parking—distinct from the Akamas Aphrodite Trail. Down to the shore, links Sea Caves–Agioi Anargyroi, then up past Aphrodite temple ruins and shepherd cave walls. Views toward Pedalio lighthouse. Cypria Aphrodite cultural route and E4 sections. Year-round.

Official circular: 7.6 km, about 3 hours, grade 2 through the Ezousa Valley from Episkopi Environmental Information Centre. Oriental plane and alder shade the river crossing; the rock church of Saint Hilarion offers views over the valley to Paphos Forest and Troodos. Winter is mild and green—a strong Paphos hills alternative to the Akamas coast.

name: Panagia tou Araka – Stavros tou Agiasmati

current.description: Official linear: 7 km, about 3 hours, grade 3 between UNESCO fresco churches at Lagoudera (Panagia tou Araka, 1192 AD) and Stavros tou Agiasmati (1494 AD). Pine forest, vineyards, and almond groves; views to Kionia, Madari, Troodos, and the Morphou plain. A 700-year oak stands at the Araka church entrance. Connects toward Madari and Lagoudera routes. Arrange transport for the linear leg.

Circular Paphos hills walk from Kathikas toward Pegeia. Two kilometres, grade 1, about 45 minutes through tall rock formations, vineyards, and a stone fountain with drinking water 800 m in. Excellent views of the Pegeia coastline on clear days.

Circular grade 3 loop outside Agios Dimitrianos with short (3 km) or long (4 km) options. Hermit cave of St Dimitrianos, the Arnies spring, vineyards, working farms, and village facilities including water and toilets.
Linear 2.5 km along the Treis Elies River—grade 1, about one hour. Medieval bridges, cherry and walnut orchards, riparian shade, and the ruins of Agios Andronicos church. Return on the same path.
Linear 2 km from the Leventis family residence through Kremmos Gorge, the Agros River, and the chapel of St George. Grade 2, about one hour. Can be made circular via the Treis Elies–Lemithou road.
Short 800 m linear path in Kato Platres forest—grade 2, about 30 minutes. Views of Limassol, Troodos National Forest Park, and Paphos Forest. Well lit; popular for an evening stroll.

Linear village connector: 4.5 km, grade 1, about 1.5 hours from Dymes to Pelendri through orchards, pine, and the Deisi locality (throne of the Virgin Mary). Drinking fountain on route. Fire damage in 2007—regrowth ongoing.
Linear 2 km between Athkies and Poullin fountains in Arsos village—grade 1, 45 minutes. River walk past medieval Panagia chapel and a traditional oil mill. Can be walked in either direction.
Circular 1.5 km loop in Kalevounari Park, Pano Polemidia—grade 1, 30 minutes. Views of the coast, western Limassol villages, and Troodos Mountains from the Polemidia picnic area.

Circular 1.3 km around the Germasogeia reservoir peninsula—grade 1, 30 minutes. Stocked fishing (permit required), native Zoulatzia bush (Bosea cypria) on the 150 m south spur. Distinct from the longer Kyparissia dam trail.
Circular 6 km from Agros—grade 2, about two hours through apple, cherry, pear, and rose (Rosa damascena) orchards. Agros rose water country; wooded sections and village road finish.

Linear 4 km, grade 2, 1.5 hours from Kalopanayiotis to Oikos via Kykkos water mill, Setrachos River, hot springs, and UNESCO Agios Ioannis Lampadistis Monastery. Stone bridge and orchard fields en route.
Linear 1 km, grade 1, 15–20 minutes from Archangelos church, Galata. Klarios riverside vegetation, Rodous mill buildings, and UNESCO Panagia Podithou church 200 m away.
Linear 6 km, grade 3, 2.5 hours from Lagoudera toward Agros through vineyards, orchards, and the Madari–Papoutsa ridge with panoramic views. Can link to Madari trail network at Adelfi Forest.
Linear 7 km, grade 3, about three hours from Agros weir area toward Madari. Panoramic ridge walking; connects to the wider Madari fire-tower network.
Linear 1.3 km through Polystypos hazelnut forest and orchards—grade 2, 30–45 minutes. Village fountain, Makroulis walnut tree, and an ~840-year oak at the trail end.
Circular grade 3 loop at Askas village entrance—about 0.5–1 hour through pine, abandoned orchards, and hazelnut groves. Pentadaktylos range views.
Circular 1.5 km, grade 3, 30 minutes in Alona (Pitsilia). Stone village scenery, cherry and apple plantations, and a Natura 2000 river reach.
Linear 3 km, grade 2, one hour from Gourri village fountain. Traditional dry-stone walls, local flora, and a natural waterfall at the trail end.
Linear 3 km, grade 3, one hour from Machairas Monastery. Crosses the Pediaios River with rich flora; E4 section linking to Lazanias–Fikardou routes.
Linear 2 km, grade 2, 45 minutes from Lazanias to UNESCO Fikardou village. Panoramic views, rich flora, E4 trail. Connects Machairas–Lazanias and Fikardou–Archontides.
Linear 5 km, grade 2, 1.5 hours from Fikardou church to Archontides. Ridge walking with Nicosia and countryside views; E4 section through rich flora.
Linear 2 km, grade 2, 45 minutes linking Choirokoitia village and the UNESCO Neolithic archaeological site. Walk from the site parking or from the village direction.
Circular 10.5 km, grade 2, 3–4 hours from Vavla village centre. Rural roads to Panagia tis Agapis church, then footpath along St Minas River and ridge roads with panoramic views.

name: Lefkara Metamorfoseos Tou Sotiros Church Trail

current.description: Circular 2.3 km, grade 2, 1.5 hours from Pano Lefkara toward Vavatsinia. Views over Pano and Kato Lefkara, Kato Drys, Dipotamos dam, and Stavrovouni. Links to Lefkara–Kato Drys path.

Linear 8.5 km, grade 1, about three hours from Profitis Ilias church (Protaras) to Konnos beach. Coastal churches, E4 parallel sections, links to Agioi Saranda, Agios Ioannis, and Konnos–Cyclops trails.
Linear 2.8 km, grade 1, 45 minutes between Panagia church (Cape Greco road) and Agios Ioannis / Agioi Saranda churches. E4 parallel sections; combine with coastal Cape Greco loops.
Linear 2.5 km, grade 1, 45 minutes from Panagia church to Agioi Saranda church near Cape Greco. Picturesque chapel, E4 parallel route.

Official Forestry circular in the heart of Paphos Forest near Stavros tis Psokas: 5 km, about 3 hours, grade 3. Calabrian pine and endemic golden oak on the climb to Chorteri peak (1,290 m). Rather difficult uphill; excellent Stavros Valley views. Mouflon and red deer enclosures at the forest station. Start 1.5 km from Stavros tis Psokas on the Kykko road.

Official Forestry circular in Agios Merkourios valley, Paphos state forest: short route 8 km (~2 h) or long 10 km (~2.5 h) on forest roads with gentle inclines. Panoramic views of Argakas Dam, Argaka village, Akamas, and Chrysochou Bay. Calabrian pine, mouflon in the SPA, and riparian pockets. Trailhead near Argaka village.

Official Forestry Yialia valley route: now circular from Nea Dimmata village square through Paphos Forest to the Symvoulas stream, Mavres–Pervoli, and Pomos (17 km, 3–5 hours). Bird's-eye views over Paphos Forest, Akamas, and Chrysochou Gulf. Named for historic forest council meetings. Linear Pomos option also documented (~11 km).

Official Forestry linear connecting three protected Venetian bridges—Elias, Tzielefos (Tzelefos), and Roudias—through Paphos Forest from Kaminaria to Vretsia. Total 17 km, 6–8 hours in four sections (3.2 + 3.9 + 6.9 + 3 km). Part of the historic Camel Road. Walk one or two sections for a half-day; full traverse needs transport at both ends.

Official Forestry circular at the Troodos Visitor Centre: 250 m, gentle incline, wheelchair accessible. Thirty labelled endemic and indigenous plants of Troodos National Forest Park—including black pine, golden oak, Troodos sage, and Cyprus cedar. Educational loop on serpentinite; ideal before Artemis or Atalante.

Cyprus's biggest carnival runs for two weeks before Lent. King Carnival leads the Grand Parade through the old town; masquerade balls fill the theatres; and the streets come alive with floats, costumes, and music. The carnival has roots in Venetian and Byzantine traditions; a last burst of revelry before the fast. Locals spend months preparing costumes. If you're in Cyprus in late February or early March, don't miss it. The energy is infectious, and the seafront promenade turns into one long party.

Eleftheria Square transforms in December: open-air concerts, food stalls, and light installations draw families and friends. Entry is free. The atmosphere is festive without being overwhelming; you can grab a hot drink, listen to live music, and watch the capital come alive after dark. It runs on weekends through the month. Wrap up and join the crowd.

The harbour fills with stalls each December. Crafts, local honey, olive oil, and handmade gifts. Mulled wine steams in the cold air. Carol singers gather by the castle. It's a family affair; children queue for Santa, parents browse the stalls, and the smell of roasting chestnuts drifts across the waterfront. Weekends from the first of December until just before Christmas. The castle is lit up. The sea is dark. It feels like the holidays in a way that sun-drenched beaches never quite manage.

The Commandaria Festival celebrates Cyprus's oldest wine—the sweet, sun-dried wine made in these hills since the Crusades. Koilani usually hosts the main events; tastings and music spread across Krasochoria and UNESCO Commandaria villages such as Louvaras, Silikou, Doros, and Monagri. Sample producers, learn how Commandaria is made, and enjoy the mountain air. Usually the first weekend of December, when the vines are bare. Check dates annually.

Cyprus has one ski resort, and it's on Mount Olympus. Four lifts, equipment hire, and mountain cafés. The season runs from January to March, depending on snow; some winters are bumper years, others are lean. Even when the pistes are thin, the drive up is rewarding and the cafés serve hot chocolate with a view. Check conditions before you go; the road can be icy. It's a novelty to ski in the morning and swim in the afternoon, and the island makes the most of it.

The village celebrates its most famous craft. Lacemakers demonstrate the Lefkaritiko technique in the square; bobbins clicking, threads crossing. Workshops let you try your hand. Stalls sell finished pieces. It's usually the second Sunday of March, when the light is already softening and the mountain air is mild. The village fills with visitors, but the mood is proud rather than commercial. These women have spent decades perfecting their craft. They're happy to show you. Stay for lunch. The tavernas do a brisk trade.

Bellapais is in north Cyprus—crossing from the south requires the usual border arrangements; verify access before you travel. Music in the Gothic ruins. Classical, folk, sometimes both. The abbey's refectory becomes a concert hall; the arches throw the sound back. You sit under the stars with the mountain at your back. The programme changes each year; check ahead for winter dates. Even if you miss a concert, the abbey at night is worth the drive when access allows.

The roses bloom in April and May. In winter, Agros works with what it has stored: rose water, loukoumi, preserves. The village hosts workshops and tastings through January and February. You can learn how rose water is made, sample the sweets, and fill a bag with souvenirs. The mountain air is cold; the tavernas are warm. Agros has built a reputation on its floral heritage. Even out of season, it's worth a visit. The factory runs tours. The views are always there.

Finikoudes Promenade turns into a winter village. An ice rink by the sea; surreal and fun. Santa's grotto for the children. Stalls selling crafts, food, and hot drinks. The palm trees stay green; the lights go up. It runs from mid-November into January, so you have plenty of chances to catch it. The promenade is Larnaca's waterfront strip. In summer it's packed. In winter it's milder, and the Christmas village adds a layer of cheer. Wrap up and stroll. The sea is right there.

Runners from across Europe gather on the Limassol seafront in December. Full marathon, half, and 10k. The route follows the coast; the weather is cool, the views are sea and sky. Even if you're not running, the atmosphere is worth experiencing. The city wakes early. The promenade fills with supporters. Cheering, music, the steady rhythm of feet. It's usually the first Sunday of December. Plan your route if you're driving; roads close for the race. Or join the crowd and watch. The finishers' faces say it all.

One of Cyprus's eight official Christmas villages. The Solea Valley village dresses up for the season: garlands, evening music, mulled wine, crafts fairs, and open-air concerts. Stone houses, the Karkotis River, and the scent of melomakarona and kourabiedes. Weekends from late November; daily from 22 December. Combine with a trout lunch or a walk to Agios Nikolaos tis Stegis. The mountain air sharpens the appetite.

High-altitude Christmas market in the Pitsilia region. Vineyards and pine forests frame the village. Traditional treats, Kyperounta winery tastings, crafts, and concerts. The mountain air. Usually 10:00–19:00; shorter hours on 25 December. About 50 minutes from Limassol. Wrap up; it's cold up there. Check dates annually.

Weekly Thursday events from January to March. Greek and international jazz, traditional Cypriot dance, rebetiko, and cultural performances. The resort's quiet season becomes a stage for music and heritage. Check the municipality programme for dates and venues—schedules vary by year. A different side of Ayia Napa.

International winter swimmers gather at Nissi or Makronissos Beach. Braving the cool sea in January. Even if you don't dive in, the spectacle is worth it—swimmers in caps, the winter light, the cheers. Dates vary; check ahead. A reminder that Cyprus never fully hibernates.

The Marathasa Valley village hosts one of the island's most atmospheric Christmas markets. Stone houses, cobbled lanes, and the UNESCO monastery of Agios Ioannis Lampadistis as a backdrop. Local products, traditional foods, music, workshops, and winter entertainment. Runs weekends from late November; daily from 23 December. Thermal springs and Byzantine frescoes nearby. A quieter alternative to Kakopetria.

The Krasochoria village of Omodos hosts a festive Christmas market in late December. The Community Park fills with stalls, live music—carols, rebetiko, jazz, folk—and workshops. Mega Santa meets children. Local products, warm wine, and handmade gifts. The cobbled square and monastery make a memorable setting. Usually 26–28 December, from 16:00. The village knows wine; expect good hospitality.

The village of lanes and vines lights up in early December. Crafts, treats, and a small-scale Christmas atmosphere. Lania is one of the fourteen authorised Commandaria villages—combine with Vasa for a wine-country day, or Omodos for Krasochoria (outside the Commandaria zone). Quieter than the big Christmas villages. The architecture and mountain views are the draw. Check dates; usually the first weekend of December.

The first day of Orthodox Lent. Families head outdoors with picnics of fasting foods—lagana bread, olives, tahini, seafood. Kite flying fills the skies; the custom is that the kite carries away sins. Parks, hills, and coastlines fill with Cypriots. Polis-Latchi and other towns host festivals. It's a public holiday. Even if you're not fasting, the ritual and the kites are worth experiencing. Dates move with Easter; typically late February or early March.

The Paralimni–Dherynia carnival brings floats, costumes, and thousands of revellers to the east coast. The grand parade rolls through Paralimni on the Sunday before Lent. Less hectic than Limassol, but no less colourful. Families line the route; the carnival king leads the procession. A regional institution. Usually early March. Arrive early for a good spot.

Christmas Strawberry Land. Deryneia—Cyprus's strawberry capital—hosts one of the eight official Christmas villages. Traditional cuisine, handmade crafts, live music, and children's workshops. The Folk Art Museum and red-soil fields frame the village. Weekends from late November; daily from 23 December. The east coast's answer to the mountain villages. Combine with Paralimni or Protaras.

High in the Paphos mountains at 950m. One of the eight official Christmas villages. Apple and grape country; the village produces wine, raisins, walnuts, almonds. Stone houses, local products, and a quiet mountain atmosphere. Chrysorrogiatissa and Agia Moni monasteries nearby. Runs from late November to Epiphany. A Paphos alternative to the Troodos villages.

Three days of Cypriot and international jazz at Rialto Theatre. Around 15 ensembles; contemporary Cypriot music, workshops, jam sessions, and after-parties. The showcase promotes local musicians to the industry and gives audiences a concentrated dose of the island's jazz scene. Usually early December. Tickets from €8 per day. A must for jazz lovers.

Greek terroirs in Cyprus. Around 25 Peloponnese wineries pour PDO and PGI wines at Carob Mill Restaurants. Masterclasses, open tastings, and professional sommeliers. A chance to taste Nemea, Mantinia, and other Greek regions without leaving the island. Usually early February. Tickets from around €10. Wine lovers take note.

A weekend of serious wine at Technopolis 20. Over 100 handpicked wines from Cyprus, Greece, Italy, and France; dozens of producers. Once trade-only, now open to enthusiasts. Two days in late January. Paphos's answer to the big Limassol tastings. Book early; it fills.

Fig Tree Bay and the Protaras waterfront light up in December. Carol singers, festive stalls, and New Year events. Quieter than summer; the palm trees and sea give the season a Mediterranean twist. Combine with Cape Greco or Konnos for a coastal day.

On January 6, Cyprus marks Epiphany; the baptism of Christ. Priests throw a wooden cross into the sea; young men dive from boats and the harbour wall to retrieve it. Whoever finds it receives a blessing for the year. The ceremony takes place at harbours and beaches across the island; Larnaca, Limassol, Paphos, and other coastal towns. Crowds gather, hymns are sung, and even in winter the bravest swimmers take the plunge. It's a public holiday, and the atmosphere is solemn and celebratory at once. Wrap up warm and arrive early for a good spot.
